Data augmentation includes additive Gaussian noise on the mean-action vector ($\sigma \in [0.02, 0.1]$) and uncertainty features ($\sigma \approx 0.006$).
The default magnitude bound is $\varepsilon = 0.2$ for all CRM variants unless stated otherwise.

\paragraph{Statistical protocol.}
Table~\ref{tab:main} reports seed 42 (10 rollouts $\times$ 10 tasks = 100 episodes per suite).
For the primary comparison, we replicate across multiple seeds on LIBERO-Object: obs\_only ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$, 6 seeds) achieves mean $17.5 \pm 2.8$\%, VLA-only (5 seeds) achieves mean $11.2 \pm 1.6$\%, and Argmin (5 seeds) achieves mean $12.4 \pm 2.9$\%.
Pooled Fisher's exact test: obs\_only vs.\ VLA-only yields $p = 0.0074$ (Cohen's $d = 1.21$).
All six obs\_only seeds exceed the VLA-only mean, confirming reproducible improvement despite per-seed variance.
Multi-seed VLA-mean evaluation (4 seeds, mean 12.5\%) confirms that averaging provides no consistent benefit over single-sample execution.


\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

Table~\ref{tab:main} compares all methods on both benchmarks.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Task success rate (\%\,$\uparrow$) on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks $\times$ 10 rollouts each, seed 42). $\Delta$ denotes improvement over the Argmin selection baseline. All methods use the same frozen SmolVLA checkpoint.}
\label{tab:main}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Method & Object (\%) & Spatial (\%) & $\Delta$ Object \\
\midrule
VLA-only ($K{=}1$)    & 12.0 & 30.0 & $\phantom{+}0.0$ \\
VLA-mean ($K{=}10$)   & 12.0 & 32.0 & $\phantom{+}0.0$ \\
Argmin ($K{=}10$)      & 12.0 & 34.0 & --- \\
\midrule
scalar ($\varepsilon{=}0.1$)  & \phantom{0}9.0 & 32.0 & $-3.0$ \\
perdof ($\varepsilon{=}0.1$)  & 11.0 & 35.0 & $-1.0$ \\
\textbf{obs\_only} ($\varepsilon{=}0.1$) & \textbf{19.0} & \textbf{35.0} & $\mathbf{+7.0}$ \\
\midrule
obs\_only ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$) & \textbf{22.0} & 35.0 & $+10.0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Object benchmark: correction helps.}
On LIBERO-Object, obs\_only at $\varepsilon{=}0.1$ achieves 19.0\% (seed 42), and at $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ yields 22.0\%.
Across six seeds ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$), the pipeline achieves mean $17.5 \pm 2.8$\% versus VLA-only mean $11.2 \pm 1.6$\% ($p = 0.0074$, pooled Fisher's exact test; Cohen's $d = 1.21$).
The improvement over Argmin (mean $12.4 \pm 2.9$\%) is +5.1\,pp.

At seed 42, three baselines (VLA-only, VLA-mean, and Argmin) all achieve 12.0\%, indicating that neither multi-sample averaging nor $L_2$ argmin selection provides meaningful benefit on this task suite.
The VLA-mean result is informative: averaging 10 independent flow-matching samples does not reduce error compared to a single sample ($K{=}1$), confirming that action diversity does not center around the correct action.
The obs\_only CRM breaks through this plateau by predicting corrective residuals conditioned on the observation embedding.

\paragraph{Pipeline decomposition: selection and correction are synergistic.}
To isolate contributions, we evaluate the CRM without multi-sample selection ($K{=}1$): the CRM corrects a single VLA output directly.
At $K{=}1$, CRM correction achieves 10.3\% (3-seed mean), at the VLA-only level (11.2\%).
Argmin selection without correction achieves 12.4\% (5-seed mean), a modest +1.2\,pp gain.
Neither component alone meaningfully improves the frozen VLA, yet the full pipeline ($K{=}10$, selection + correction) achieves 17.5\%, a +6.3\,pp gain ($p = 0.0074$).
This synergy arises because argmin selection filters out the worst samples, providing the CRM with a higher-quality starting point; the CRM then applies corrections that are more reliable on these pre-screened candidates.
In terms of contribution decomposition: selection accounts for ${\sim}$1\,pp and correction for ${\sim}$5\,pp, with correction 4--5$\times$ more valuable than selection alone.

\paragraph{Spatial benchmark: correction does not help.}
On LIBERO-Spatial, all methods cluster within a 5\,pp band (30--35\%).
The best CRM variants (obs\_only, perdof) achieve 35\%, only 1\,pp above the Argmin baseline (34\%).
This is a null result that we report prominently.

We interpret this as follows: spatial perturbations in LIBERO-Spatial involve changes to object layout (e.g., moving target locations), which may require re-planning rather than local action correction.
The VLA's observation encoder cannot extract correctable error signals from spatial shifts. The problem is not that actions are inaccurate given the current state, but that the task structure itself has changed.
Residual correction at the action level is the wrong granularity for this type of generalization.

\paragraph{Key finding.}
The full pipeline significantly improves over VLA-only for object manipulation ($p < 0.01$), where the challenge is fine-grained motor control with novel objects.
For spatial reasoning, where the challenge is planning under layout changes, correction at the action level provides no benefit over selection alone.


\subsection{CRM Conditioning Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}

We focus the conditioning ablation on LIBERO-Object, where meaningful differences emerge (Table~\ref{tab:main}).

\paragraph{Ranking.}
obs\_only (19.0\%) $\gg$ Argmin (12.0\%) $\approx$ perdof (11.0\%) $>$ scalar (9.0\%).

This ordering is the central negative result of our ablation: per-DOF conformal features, despite being intuitively richer (40 additional dimensions capturing per-DOF standard deviations, conformal radii, and log-volume terms), \emph{hurt} rather than help.
Scalar uncertainty conditioning (3 additional dimensions) performs even worse, falling 3.0\,pp below the Argmin baseline that uses no correction at all.

The scalar $<$ perdof ordering is consistent across seeds (scalar: 9\%/6\% for seeds 42/44; perdof: 11\%/8\%).
One-dimensional scalar uncertainty compresses all six action dimensions into a single number.
When certain dimensions carry high uncertainty but the correction direction is already correct along those axes, the scalar signal cannot distinguish this case from one where correction is needed everywhere.
The result is uniform over-correction or under-correction across all dimensions.
Per-DOF conditioning at least permits dimension-specific judgments, though at $K{=}10$ these judgments remain too noisy to be useful.
Even 1D scalar uncertainty conditioning is harmful, confirming that conformal scores at $K{=}10$ are unreliable regardless of aggregation dimensionality.
The noise originates in the score itself (rank-deficient covariance estimate from 10 samples in 6D), not in how these scores are decomposed across dimensions.

\paragraph{Why does richer conditioning fail?}
We identify three factors:

\emph{(1) Noisy covariance estimation.}
With $K{=}10$ samples in $d{=}6$ dimensions, the dimension-to-sample ratio is $d/K = 0.6$.
While Ledoit--Wolf shrinkage~\cite{ledoit2004well} stabilizes the covariance estimate for selection (Section~\ref{sec:selection}), the per-DOF features derived from this estimate (standard deviations, conformal radii) still carry substantial estimation noise.
Feeding these noisy features as CRM input introduces a distribution shift between training data (where noise patterns are consistent) and closed-loop evaluation (where compounding state-distribution drift produces different noise patterns).

\emph{(2) Observation features are sufficient.}
The frozen VLA observation embedding $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{obs}} \in \mathbb{R}^{960}$ already encodes task-relevant geometric information: object identity, spatial layout, gripper-object relationship, and task progress.
This information subsumes what the per-DOF conformal features attempt to capture, namely which action dimensions are uncertain given the current scene.
The CRM learns to map directly from scene understanding to corrective residuals, without the intermediate conformal statistics.

\emph{(3) Per-step MSE $\neq$ episode success.}
All CRM variants achieve low per-step MSE on held-out demonstration data, yet offline prediction accuracy does not predict closed-loop task success.
In closed-loop evaluation, small per-step errors compound and the robot visits states far from the demonstration distribution~\cite{ross2011dagger}.
The noisy conformal features amplify this drift: occasional erroneous correction directions, even when small in magnitude, can trigger cascading failures in individual episodes.

\paragraph{Connection to magnitude sensitivity.}
The obs\_only variant is also more robust across magnitude bounds $\varepsilon$ than perdof (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude_results}), providing further evidence that observation-only conditioning yields a more stable correction signal.


\subsection{Magnitude Sensitivity}
\label{sec:magnitude_results}

The norm bound $\varepsilon$ determines how much CRM can deviate from the conformal-selected action.
Figure~\ref{fig:magnitude} shows performance across $\varepsilon \in [0.03, 1.42]$ on both benchmarks.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/magnitude_curve.pdf}
\caption{Success rate (\%) as a function of magnitude bound $\varepsilon$. \textbf{(a)}~LIBERO-Object: obs\_only (solid blue) stays above both baselines across all tested $\varepsilon$; error bars show $\pm$1 std over available seeds (n annotated). perdof (dashed red) collapses below the Argmin baseline at $\varepsilon \geq 0.2$. Shaded region marks the recommended range $\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.2]$. \textbf{(b)}~LIBERO-Spatial (seed 42): obs\_only maintains 35--36\% across all $\varepsilon$, while perdof drops to 0\% without magnitude control ($\varepsilon{\approx}1.42$).}
\label{fig:magnitude}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Success rate (\%) on LIBERO-Spatial across magnitude bounds $\varepsilon$. The Argmin baseline (34\%, no correction) is independent of $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:magnitude}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
$\varepsilon$ & 0.05 & 0.1 & 0.3 & 1.42 \\
\midrule
obs\_only & 35.0 & 35.0 & 36.0 & --- \\
perdof    & 31.0 & 35.0 & 26.0 & 0.0 \\
\midrule
Argmin (ref.) & \multicolumn{4}{c}{34.0 (flat, no correction)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{obs\_only is robust.}
The obs\_only variant maintains 35--36\% across the full range $\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.3]$, a remarkably flat profile.
This stability means the practitioner need not carefully tune $\varepsilon$; any value in $[0.05, 0.2]$ yields near-identical performance.

\paragraph{perdof is fragile.}
In contrast, perdof peaks at 35\% when $\varepsilon{=}0.1$ but collapses to 26\% at $\varepsilon{=}0.3$ (a 9\,pp drop).
This fragility suggests that the noisy conformal features cause the CRM to predict unreliable correction directions; when the magnitude bound is loose enough to accommodate these directions, performance degrades.
At $\varepsilon{=}0.1$, the tight bound masks the problem by clipping erroneous corrections.

\paragraph{Unbounded correction is catastrophic.}
Without magnitude control ($\varepsilon{\approx}1.42$, the natural CRM output norm), perdof achieves 0\% on LIBERO-Spatial. Compounding error across the trajectory destroys performance entirely (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude}).
The Argmin baseline (34\%) outperforms all CRM variants at this setting, demonstrating that unbounded correction is harmful.
The obs\_only variant was not evaluated at $\varepsilon{=}1.42$ on spatial, though analogous catastrophic failure is expected given the magnitude of unconstrained corrections.

\paragraph{Practical recommendation.}
The safe operating range is $\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.2]$.
Within this range, obs\_only is the only variant that never degrades below the Argmin baseline across all tested seeds and magnitude bounds.
We use $\varepsilon{=}0.1$ as the default, which provides a conservative margin below the point where perdof begins to degrade.


\subsection{Per-Task Analysis}
\label{sec:per_task}

Table~\ref{tab:pertask} reports per-task success rates on LIBERO-Object (seed 42) for the VLA-only baseline, Argmin selection, and obs\_only at two magnitude bounds.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Per-task success rate (\%) on LIBERO-Object (seed 42, 10 rollouts per task). Tasks ordered by obs\_only $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ improvement over VLA-only.}
\label{tab:pertask}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Task & VLA-only & Argmin & obs\_only 0.1 & obs\_only 0.2 \\
\midrule
chocolate\_pudding & 20 & 30 & 50 & 60 \\
ketchup            &  0 &  0 & 10 & 20 \\
bbq\_sauce         & 20 & 30 & 40 & 40 \\
salad\_dressing    & 20 & 10 & 20 & 30 \\
butter             &  0 & 10 & 10 & 10 \\
milk               & 10 & 10 & 20 & 20 \\
orange\_juice      & 30 & 30 & 30 & 30 \\
tomato\_sauce      & 10 &  0 &  0 & 10 \\
alphabet\_soup     &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 \\
cream\_cheese      & 10 &  0 & 10 &  0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Improvement concentrates on medium-difficulty tasks.}
The +10\,pp aggregate gain of obs\_only ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$) over VLA-only is not uniformly distributed across tasks.
The largest improvements appear on tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors: chocolate\_pudding (+40\,pp, from 20\% to 60\%), bbq\_sauce and ketchup (+20\,pp each), and salad\_dressing (+10\,pp).
These four tasks account for 9 of the 10 additional successes.
Conversely, four tasks (alphabet\_soup, cream\_cheese, tomato\_sauce, butter) remain at 0--10\% across all methods, including obs\_only.
For these tasks, the base policy fails so completely that local action-level correction cannot recover a viable trajectory.

\paragraph{Implications for the correction mechanism.}
Correction benefits tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors, rather than tasks where the base policy fails catastrophically or already succeeds reliably.
This pattern is expected for a residual correction approach bounded by $\varepsilon$: the CRM can fix small deviations in grasp pose or approach angle, but cannot recover from fundamental planning failures (e.g., reaching toward the wrong object entirely).
The concentrated improvement profile also addresses the question of effect size: the aggregate +10\,pp is not a uniform +1\,pp across 10 tasks, but a substantial +20--40\,pp on specific tasks diluted by tasks outside the correctable regime.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate the Conformal Refinement Module (CRM) on LIBERO-Object to answer four questions:
(1)~Where does the improvement originate, multi-sample selection or learned correction?
(2)~How does CRM conditioning interact with correction magnitude?
(3)~Does performance scale with the number of VLA samples $K$?
(4)~Does the approach transfer to tokenized VLAs?
In brief: correction contributes 4--5$\times$ more than selection (\S\ref{sec:component}); observation-only conditioning is robust across magnitudes while conformal conditioning collapses (\S\ref{sec:magnitude_interaction}); performance increases monotonically from $K{=}1$ to $K{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:kvalue}); and tokenized VLAs lack the sampling diversity that multi-sample refinement requires (\S\ref{sec:applicability}).


\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:exp_setup}

\paragraph{Benchmark.}
We use LIBERO-Object~\cite{liu2023libero}, a suite of 10 tabletop manipulation tasks requiring generalization to novel object instances.
Each task is evaluated over 10 rollouts (maximum 300 steps), for 100 episodes per method per seed.
Success is binary: the task predicate must be satisfied before the step limit.

\paragraph{Base VLA.}
We build on SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla}, a 0.4B-parameter flow-matching VLA.
The model receives dual-camera RGB input (agentview + eye-in-hand, $256{\times}256$) and 8D proprioceptive state, and outputs 7D actions (6D end-effector pose + 1D gripper).
The gripper dimension is handled via direct thresholding, outside the refinement pipeline.

\paragraph{Baselines.}
All methods share the same frozen SmolVLA checkpoint:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{VLA-only} ($K{=}1$): single VLA sample, no selection or correction.
  \item \textbf{Random sel.}\ ($K{=}10$): one uniformly random sample from 10 candidates.
  \item \textbf{Argmin sel.}\ ($K{=}10$): candidate closest to the sample mean (L2 distance), no correction.
  \item \textbf{VLA-mean} ($K{=}10$): mean of 10 independent flow-matching samples.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{CRM variants.}
Three CRM variants share the same 3-layer MLP (${\sim}$337K parameters) and differ only in conditioning input:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{obs\_only}: frozen VLA observation embedding $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{obs}} \in \mathbb{R}^{960}$. Does \emph{not} use conformal statistics. This is our primary method.
  \item \textbf{perdof}: $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ concatenated with 40D per-DOF conformal features (standard deviations, conformal radii, log-volume terms).
  \item \textbf{scalar}: $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ concatenated with 1D scalar uncertainty.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Statistical protocol.}
Each condition is evaluated with 2--6 seeds (100 rollouts per seed).
We report mean $\pm$ standard deviation across seeds.
For the primary comparison, we apply a one-sided Fisher exact test on pooled rollout counts and report Cohen's $d$ as the effect size measure.


%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Main Results: Component Decomposition}
\label{sec:component}

Table~\ref{tab:component} decomposes the full pipeline into selection and correction stages.
The three non-CRM multi-sample methods (random, argmin, VLA-mean) cluster within 11--13\%, % exp_id: \S2C, \S2D
at most 1.3\,pp above VLA-only. % exp_id: \S2C
Only obs\_only CRM breaks out of this band.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Component decomposition on LIBERO-Object (100 rollouts per seed).
Bold: best; underline: second best.
$^\dagger$Partial data: 7/10 tasks completed, seed\,42 only.
$^\ddagger$Best $\varepsilon$ per variant.}
\label{tab:component}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccrl@{}}
\toprule
Method & SR (\%) $\uparrow$ & Seeds & $\Delta$ & Component \\
\midrule
VLA-only ($K{=}1$)
  & $11.2 \pm 1.6$  & 5 & ---     & Baseline \\      % exp_id: \S2C
Random sel.\ ($K{=}10$)$^\dagger$
  & ${\sim}11.4$     & 1 & $+0.2$  & ---      \\      % exp_id: \S2C, partial seed42
Argmin sel.\ ($K{=}10$)
  & $12.4 \pm 2.9$  & 5 & $+1.2$  & + Selection \\   % exp_id: \S2C
VLA-mean ($K{=}10$)
  & $\underline{12.5 \pm 2.1}$ & 4 & $+1.3$ & + Aggregation \\ % exp_id: \S2C
\midrule
CRM scalar$^\ddagger$ ($K{=}10$)
  & $8.3 \pm 2.1$   & 3 & $-2.9$  & + Correction \\  % exp_id: \S2C
CRM perdof$^\ddagger$ ($K{=}10$, $\varepsilon{=}0.1$)
  & $11.0 \pm 2.0$  & 6 & $-0.2$  & + Correction \\  % exp_id: \S2C
\textbf{CRM obs\_only} ($K{=}10$, $\varepsilon{=}0.2$)
  & $\mathbf{17.5 \pm 2.8}$ & \textbf{6} & $\mathbf{+6.3}$ & \textbf{+ Correction} \\ % exp_id: \S2C
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Selection contributes ${\sim}$1\,pp; correction contributes ${\sim}$5\,pp.}
Argmin selection adds only ${\sim}$1\,pp over random selection ($12.4\%$ vs ${\sim}11.4\%$), % exp_id: \S2D
confirming that L2-to-mean ranking provides a weak signal at $K{=}10$.
The obs\_only CRM then adds ${\sim}$5\,pp on top of argmin ($17.5\%$ vs $12.4\%$), % exp_id: \S2D
so correction is 4--5$\times$ more valuable than selection. % exp_id: \S2D

This result is statistically reliable.
obs\_only vs VLA-only yields Fisher exact $p = 0.0074$ (one-sided) with Cohen's $d = 1.21$; % exp_id: \S2E
obs\_only vs argmin yields a paired $t$-test $p = 0.016$. % exp_id: \S2E

\paragraph{Negative results: conformal conditioning hurts.}
The perdof variant ($11.0\%$) performs no better than VLA-only despite receiving 40 additional conformal features, % exp_id: \S2C
and scalar ($8.3\%$) is 2.9\,pp \emph{worse} than the uncorrected baseline. % exp_id: \S2C
With $K{=}10$ samples in $d{=}6$ dimensions, per-DOF covariance estimates carry substantial noise.
The obs\_only variant avoids this failure mode by conditioning solely on the VLA observation embedding, which already encodes task-relevant geometric information (object identity, gripper-object relationship, task progress) without the intermediate conformal statistics.


%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Conditioning-Magnitude Interaction}
\label{sec:magnitude_interaction}

The norm bound $\varepsilon$ (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude}) controls how far the CRM can deviate from the selected action.
Table~\ref{tab:magnitude} and Figure~\ref{fig:magnitude} reveal a sharp contrast between obs\_only and perdof across the magnitude range.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Success rate (\%) on LIBERO-Object across correction magnitudes $\varepsilon$.
Seed count in parentheses.
Bold marks the overall best.
The VLA-only baseline ($11.2\%$, independent of $\varepsilon$) is shown for reference.}
\label{tab:magnitude}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
\toprule
$\varepsilon$ & 0.03 & 0.05 & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & uncapped \\
\midrule
obs\_only
  & 16.0\,(1) & 13.5\,(2) & 15.3\,(4) & \textbf{17.5}\,(6) & 17.0\,(4) & 14.3\,(3) \\ % exp_id: \S2A
perdof
  & 14.0\,(1) & 14.0\,(1) & 11.0\,(6) & 9.8\,(6) & 4.7\,(3) & 0.0\,(3) \\              % exp_id: \S2A
\midrule
VLA-only
  & \multicolumn{6}{c}{$11.2 \pm 1.6$ (flat, no correction)} \\                           % exp_id: \S2C
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/magnitude_curve.pdf}
\caption{Success rate vs correction magnitude $\varepsilon$ on LIBERO-Object.
obs\_only (blue) stays above the VLA-only baseline at every tested $\varepsilon$.
perdof (red) collapses from 14\% at small $\varepsilon$ to 0\% when uncapped.
Error bars: $\pm$1 std; seed counts annotated per point.}
\label{fig:magnitude}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{obs\_only is robust across magnitudes.}
obs\_only stays above VLA-only at every tested $\varepsilon$, % exp_id: \S2A
with performance in a narrow band from 13.5\% ($\varepsilon{=}0.05$) to 17.5\% ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$). % exp_id: \S2A
Even uncapped ($\varepsilon \approx 1.42$), it achieves 14.3\%, % exp_id: \S2A
still 3.1\,pp above VLA-only. % exp_id: \S2A, \S2C
A practitioner need not carefully tune $\varepsilon$: any value in $[0.03, 0.3]$ yields consistent improvement.

\paragraph{perdof collapses progressively.}
perdof declines monotonically as $\varepsilon$ grows: $14.0 \to 14.0 \to 11.0 \to 9.8 \to 4.7 \to 0.0$. % exp_id: \S2A
At small $\varepsilon$, the tight norm bound clips erroneous corrections and masks the noisy conformal features.
As $\varepsilon$ increases, the CRM applies larger corrections along unreliable directions, and compounding error across the trajectory destroys performance.
All three uncapped perdof seeds score 0/100 successes. % exp_id: \S2H

This interaction is the central diagnostic: the same architecture succeeds or fails based on whether it receives clean (observation-only) or noisy (conformal) conditioning.
The magnitude bound does not rescue a poorly conditioned CRM; it only delays the collapse.


%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Inference-Time Scaling (K-Value Curve)}
\label{sec:kvalue}

Figure~\ref{fig:kvalue} plots task success rate as a function of the number of VLA samples $K$ for obs\_only at $\varepsilon{=}0.2$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/k_value_curve.pdf}
\caption{Success rate vs number of VLA samples $K$ for obs\_only ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$) on LIBERO-Object.
Performance increases monotonically from $K{=}1$ to $K{=}10$.
Error bars: $\pm$1 std where multiple seeds are available.
$^*$Single seed (seed\,42).}
\label{fig:kvalue}
\end{figure}

At $K{=}1$, the CRM corrects a single VLA output without multi-sample selection and achieves $10.3\% \pm 1.5\%$ ($n{=}3$), % exp_id: \S2B
indistinguishable from VLA-only ($11.2\%$). % exp_id: \S2C
At $K{=}5$, performance rises to $14.0\%$ (single seed$^*$, seed\,42). % exp_id: \S2B
At $K{=}10$, the full pipeline reaches $17.5\% \pm 2.8\%$ ($n{=}6$). % exp_id: \S2B
The trend is monotonic: $10.3\% \to 14.0\% \to 17.5\%$. % exp_id: \S2B

More VLA samples improve the argmin starting point: with larger $K$, the selected candidate sits closer to the sample centroid and, on average, closer to the demonstration action.
The CRM correction is then more effective because smaller residuals keep the output within the reliable regime of the learned MLP.

The $K{=}1$ result is the critical control.
It confirms that correction alone, without multi-sample selection, provides no measurable benefit over the uncorrected VLA.
The CRM does not learn a fixed correction bias independent of sample quality; the improvement requires both a good starting point from selection and a learned residual from the CRM.


%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Applicability Boundary: Tokenized VLAs}
\label{sec:applicability}

The multi-sample pipeline requires diverse action candidates from the base VLA.
We test this prerequisite on OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla}, a 7B-parameter autoregressive VLA based on Llama-2.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/diversity_analysis.pdf}
\caption{Action sample diversity comparison.
SmolVLA (flow-matching) produces diverse candidates across flow trajectories.
OpenVLA (autoregressive, $T{=}0.5$) generates near-identical samples: 8/10 are identical with per-DOF variance $< 10^{-30}$.}
\label{fig:diversity}
\end{figure}

At standard temperature $T{=}0.5$, OpenVLA's $K{=}10$ samples are near-deterministic: % exp_id: \S2G
8 of 10 are identical, with per-DOF variance below $10^{-30}$. % exp_id: \S2G
Multi-sample selection over identical candidates reduces to random selection, and the CRM receives the same input regardless of $K$.

Raising $T$ to 1.5 or above increases diversity but degrades the base policy. % exp_id: \S2G
No temperature setting achieves both sufficient diversity and acceptable base performance. % exp_id: \S2G

The multi-sample refinement pipeline is therefore specific to stochastic VLA architectures (e.g., flow-matching models) that produce naturally diverse candidates at their standard operating point.
Tokenized autoregressive VLAs would require alternative candidate generation strategies, such as latent-space perturbation or ensemble decoding.
